contentSections.synthesis: The defining property of a held-out set is that failing cases don't get individually diagnosed and specifically patched — if the pattern that emerges is 'the agent is weak on X category,' a general fix for X is fair game, but chasing the literal failing case defeats the entire purpose, regardless of how infrequently it's checked.

contentSections.body: In practice, most teams — especially a solo builder or a small team without the volume for a rigorous statistical split — won't run a formal held-out set the way a large ML team would. The practical version that still captures the value: **occasionally test against real, fresh cases that weren't part of any prompt-tuning cycle, and when they fail, ask whether the failure represents a pattern worth a general fix, rather than immediately patching that literal case and moving on.** The discipline being protected isn't the specific ceremony — it's the honesty of not letting the number you report be built entirely out of cases the agent has effectively been trained, case by case, to pass.

A held-out set stops doing its job the moment individual failures on it get diagnosed and specifically patched — it needs to catch patterns worth a general fix, not become a second development set on a slower cycle.

title: Build eval cases for seven agents
description: Seven drills applying this module's full toolkit — real-failure sourcing, the boring/hard/adversarial split, coverage judgment, honest maintenance, and held-out discipline — to new agents.

learningObjectives.text: Apply eval-set sourcing, coverage, and honesty judgment to new agent scenarios

contentSections.title: Seven drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against eval-set scenarios you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: source cases from real failures across all three bands, grow coverage rather than raw count, never edit a case just because it keeps failing, and check progress against cases you haven't tuned against.

title: Build a thirty-case eval set
description: Assemble a thirty-case eval set for a real agent task, sourced from real failures across all three bands, with a documented sourcing rationale and a held-out slice.

learningObjectives.text: Assemble a thirty-case eval set with documented sourcing and band coverage across boring, hard, and adversarial input

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every idea in this module — real failures over imagined ones, covering all three bands, matching coverage to raw count, keeping the set honest under pressure, and holding some cases back — was building toward one concrete artifact: an actual thirty-case eval set for a real agent task, with a written record of where each case came from and why.

contentSections.title: A thirty-case eval set with documented sourcing and band coverage
contentSections.brief: Pick a real agent task — ideally the same one from the previous module's lab, or any agent task you can describe concretely. Assemble thirty eval cases covering boring, hard, and adversarial input, sourced from real data, real failure reports, or teammates where possible rather than invented from scratch. Set aside a held-out slice you commit not to individually tune against.
contentSections.deliverable: A thirty-case eval set (each case: input, expected outcome, band classification, and a one-line sourcing note — where this case came from and why it's real rather than imagined), split into a development slice and a held-out slice, with a short document explaining the sourcing and coverage decisions.

stages.title: Source and classify the cases
stages.instructions: Gather cases from at least two real sources (production data, bug reports, a teammate trying to break it, your own prior manual testing that surfaced a real issue) — minimize purely-imagined cases. For each case, write the input, the expected outcome, and classify it as boring, hard, or adversarial (lessons one and two).
stages.checkpoint: At least 20 cases gathered from real sources with a sourcing note each, roughly matching real-world proportions across the three bands rather than all one band.

stages.title: Check coverage, not just count, and split off a held-out slice
stages.instructions: Review the set for near-duplicate cases that test the same thing repeatedly rather than adding real coverage (lesson three), and consolidate or diversify where needed to reach thirty genuinely distinct cases. Set aside roughly 20% of the set as a held-out slice, chosen before you look closely at how the agent currently performs on them (lesson five).
stages.checkpoint: Thirty cases with minimal near-duplication, and a clearly marked held-out slice set aside before close inspection.

stages.title: Run it, and write the honesty rules you'll follow
stages.instructions: Run the agent against the development slice. For any failing case, write down what a general fix (not a fix scoped to that case's literal wording) would look like, without necessarily implementing it yet. Write one paragraph committing to when a case is and isn't allowed to be removed from the set (lesson four), and how the held-out slice will actually be protected from individual tuning (lesson five).
stages.checkpoint: A results summary from the development slice, at least one general (not literal-case-scoped) fix direction identified, and a written honesty commitment for both case removal and held-out protection.

stages.title: Self-check against the rubric
stages.instructions: Re-read the full set against the rubric below before calling it done.
stages.checkpoint: Every rubric criterion below is met, or you've noted specifically why one isn't yet and what would close the gap.

rubric.criterion: The majority of cases come from real sources, not pure imagination
rubric.meets: Most cases are sourced from real data, real bug reports, or someone other than the builder attempting to find failures — each with a one-line sourcing note.

rubric.criterion: All three bands are represented
rubric.meets: Boring, hard, and adversarial cases are all present, in proportions that roughly reflect the task's real traffic rather than one band dominating by default.

rubric.criterion: The thirty cases represent genuinely distinct situations
rubric.meets: No band is padded mostly with near-duplicate variations of one scenario; each case adds real, distinguishable coverage.

rubric.criterion: A held-out slice exists and was set aside honestly
rubric.meets: Roughly 20% of the set was set aside before close inspection of how the agent performs on it, and the document states how it will be protected from individual case-tuning going forward.

rubric.criterion: Any identified fix targets the general category, not the literal case
rubric.meets: For at least one failing case, the fix direction described addresses the pattern the case represents, not just that case's exact wording.

rubric.criterion: The document is honest about gaps
rubric.meets: Where coverage is thin or a case's classification is debatable, the document says so rather than presenting the set as more complete than it is.

contentSections.body: A thirty-case eval set only does its job if most of it came from reality rather than imagination, covers all three bands, and keeps a slice honestly untouched — this lab exists to produce that, not a tidy-looking list that happens to total thirty.

title: Checkpoint — Building an Eval Set
description: Ungraded retrieval: 4 from this module, 4 from What "Works" Means Here, 2 from Keeping Control.

learningObjectives.text: Recall this module's eval-set vocabulary and how it connects to success-criteria and control concepts from earlier in the track

contentSections.title: Let's see what stuck
Checkpoint — Building an Eval Set

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Set

options.label: The imagined cases reflect the builder's mental model of the task, not the actual range of messy real input
Imagined cases are always fine as long as there are enough of them
The agent must have a bug unrelated to the eval set

questions.explanation: Lesson one — cases written entirely from one person's imagination sample from that person's mental model of 'typical' input, which systematically misses the messiness real data actually contains.

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Set

options.label: It has no boring/typical cases in it, so a regression in the ordinary input that makes up most real traffic has nothing there to catch it
Hard cases are never actually useful to test
There's no blind spot — hard cases are the most rigorous kind to test

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Set

options.label: Raw count went up far more than real coverage did — those 55 cases mostly test one situation repeatedly
This is a genuine quadrupling of coverage
Near-duplicate cases should never be included under any circumstances

questions.from: This module — Building an Eval Set
questions.prompt: A team deletes a case that's failed for months right before a stakeholder demo, calling it cleanup. What's actually happening?

options.label: The eval set is being edited to make the number look better, not because the case stopped being a real, relevant failure
This is legitimate maintenance since the failure is already known
This is fine as long as the team privately remembers the case existed

questions.from: Two modules back — What "Works" Means Here

options.label: How much the resulting claim will be relied on and what it costs to be wrong, not a fixed universal number
Always exactly ten runs, regardless of the decision
As few as possible, to save time

questions.explanation: From What "Works" Means Here, lesson five — a rough internal gut-check tolerates a handful of runs; a public claim or a ship decision deserves far more, matched to what's actually riding on it.

questions.from: Two modules back — What "Works" Means Here

options.label: Whether the path taken to reach the result was sound — right tools, no unnecessary or risky actions — independent of whether the end-state was correct
Only the dollar cost of the run
Nothing — process and outcome always move together

questions.explanation: From What "Works" Means Here, lesson three — a run can reach a correct end-state via an unsound path (wrong APIs called, unnecessary access), and only a separate process measure catches that.

options.label: Repeated runs of the case both before and after the change, compared as rates, not a single before-run and a single after-run
Nothing further — a single passing run after any change is sufficient proof
Running a completely different case instead of the original failing one

questions.explanation: From What "Works" Means Here, lesson four — a single run is one draw from a distribution; only a real before-rate and after-rate, from repeated runs, show whether the rate actually moved.

options.label: It's a true but small, self-selected sample — real, just not enough of it, and drawn from friendlier inputs than real usage
It's entirely fabricated and doesn't describe anything that actually happened
It's actually strong evidence, not weak evidence

Any action the agent performs more than once a day
Only actions that involve sending money

questions.explanation: From Keeping Control — the bar for requiring human approval is about the severity and reversibility of a wrong outcome, not about frequency or a narrow category like payments alone.

questions.from: Three modules back — Keeping Control
questions.prompt: That module argued auditability means proving what an agent did and why. What made that different from just having logs?

options.label: Auditability requires the reasoning behind a decision to be reconstructable, not just the fact that an action occurred
Auditability is identical to logging — any log file satisfies it
Auditability only applies to financial transactions

questions.explanation: From Keeping Control — proving what happened and proving why it happened are different claims; auditability needs the second, which plain action logs alone don't guarantee.

title: Exact match, and everything it can't grade
description: Where exact-match and simple pattern grading genuinely work, and the large territory of agent output where they silently fail.

learningObjectives.text: Identify tasks where exact-match grading is a sound, sufficient approach
Explain why exact-match grading fails silently on open-ended or free-text output

contentSections.title: A grader that scores a good answer zero

contentSections.body: A team building a customer-question-answering agent writes a quick grader: compare the agent's answer, as a string, against a reference answer written for each eval case. For "What's your return window?" the reference answer is "30 days from the date of purchase." The agent answers "You have 30 days from your purchase date to return it." The grader scores it 0 — the strings don't match — even though the answer is correct.

contentSections.scenario: The team is confused: the grader says fail, a human reading both answers says obviously pass.
contentSections.question: What's actually wrong here?

options.label: The agent's answer is subtly wrong in a way the human reviewer missed
Exact-string-match grading was applied to a task where correctness isn't about matching one exact phrasing — the same correct fact can be stated many different, equally valid ways
The reference answer was written incorrectly

feedback.wrong-grader: Right. The agent's answer and the reference answer say the same thing in different words — that's not a grading edge case, it's the normal shape of free-text output. An exact-match grader was never going to handle that.
feedback.agent-wrong: There's nothing wrong with the agent's answer here — it states the same policy correctly, just in different words. The mismatch is entirely in the grader, not the agent.
feedback.bad-reference: The reference answer is fine on its own terms — the problem isn't that it's wrong, it's that treating it as the one acceptable string, rather than one example of a correct answer, is the wrong grading approach for this kind of output.

contentSections.mechanism: Exact-match grading checks whether an output equals a specific string (or matches a narrow pattern) — it works when there's genuinely one correct form the answer must take, and fails the instant a task has more than one valid way to say the same correct thing, which is most free-text output.

contentSections.body:
Exact-match grading isn't a bad idea — it's a narrow tool, correctly used only where the task itself has a single correct form:

- A calculation with one right numeric answer.
- A classification into one of a fixed set of labels.
- Whether a specific required field (an order number, a status code) is present and correctly formatted.
- Whether an action happened or didn't (a file was written, an API was called with the right arguments).

Where it silently breaks: anything where the *meaning* matters more than the *exact wording* — a summary, an explanation, a drafted email, an answer to an open-ended question. There, two different agents (or the same agent on two different runs) can both be fully correct while producing text that shares almost no exact wording. Grading those with string match doesn't just occasionally miss — it structurally can't succeed, because it's checking the wrong thing entirely.
Exact-match grading works when a task has one correct form — it fails structurally, not occasionally, on anything where meaning matters more than exact wording.

contentSections.title: The grading gap doesn't announce itself

contentSections.body: The same team, after noticing the return-window problem, patches their grader to check for keyword presence instead: does the answer contain the substring "30 days"? An agent answer that says "Returns are accepted within a month of purchase" — also correct — scores 0, because it never says the literal digits "30."

contentSections.question: The team is tempted to keep patching: add "a month," then "one month," then "four weeks" to the accepted-phrasing list every time a new correct-but-differently-worded answer slips through. Where does that road actually lead?
contentSections.answer: Nowhere good, and never to "done." The space of correct ways to phrase "you have 30 days" is effectively open-ended — new valid phrasings keep showing up as long as people keep writing new answers. A growing keyword list is trying to enumerate an open-ended set one item at a time, which is the signal to switch to a meaning-based grading approach, not to add one more pattern.
contentSections.hint: Ask whether the list of 'acceptable phrasings' for one simple fact ever actually reaches a final, complete state.

contentSections.body:
This is the trap inside the trap: patching exact-match with a slightly looser check (substring, keyword presence, a regex) usually just relocates the same failure to a smaller, still-real set of correct-but-differently-worded answers. It can feel like progress — the pass rate ticks up — without actually reaching the root cause, which is that **grading free-text meaning requires understanding the meaning**, not pattern-matching the surface form.

The honest signal that a task has outgrown exact/pattern matching: when writing a grader, if you find yourself adding case after case of "also accept this phrasing... and this one... and this one" to a growing regex or keyword list, that list is trying to enumerate the space of correct phrasings one at a time — a space that's usually open-ended. That's the point to reach for a different grading approach entirely (rubric grading and model-as-judge, the next two lessons), rather than the point to add one more pattern.
A growing list of 'also accept this phrasing' patches to a grader is a sign the task needs a meaning-based grading approach, not one more pattern.

title: Rubrics a grader can apply consistently
description: Writing a rubric specific enough that two different graders — human or model — apply it the same way to the same output.

learningObjectives.text: Write a rubric with criteria specific enough to be applied consistently
Identify when a rubric criterion is too subjective to grade consistently

contentSections.title: "Sounds professional" gets graded three different ways

contentSections.body: A rubric for grading drafted customer emails has one line: "Sounds professional (0-5)." Three team members grade the same email independently: one gives it a 5, one a 3 ("a bit stiff"), one a 4. Nobody's grading is wrong, exactly — there's just nothing in the rubric that says what 'professional' actually requires.

contentSections.scenario:
Two candidate rubric criteria for the same email-drafting task:

A. "Sounds professional (0-5)"
B. "Contains a greeting and sign-off (1 point), makes no unsubstantiated claims not present in the source brief (1 point), uses no exclamation points or all-caps words (1 point), states the main ask or answer within the first two sentences (1 point)"
contentSections.question: Which is more likely to produce the same score from two different graders?

options.label: A
B

feedback.b: Right. Each sub-point in B checks something concrete and countable — present or absent — rather than asking the grader to weigh an overall impression.
feedback.a: A single 0-5 scale on an undefined word like 'professional' asks each grader to invent their own definition on the spot, which is exactly what produced three different scores for the same email.

contentSections.concept: A **consistent rubric** breaks a vague quality into concrete, checkable sub-criteria — each one closer to a yes/no or a count than to an overall impression — so that two different graders applying it independently land on close to the same score.

contentSections.body:
The instinct to write "sounds professional (0-5)" is reasonable — professionalism is a real thing that matters — but a single scalar score on an undefined quality asks every grader to silently supply their own definition, and different graders' definitions won't match. The fix isn't to abandon the quality, it's to decompose it into the concrete signals that actually make an email read as professional: a greeting and sign-off present, no unsubstantiated claims, no shouting-register punctuation, the point stated early rather than buried. Each of those is checkable on its own, and the total score becomes the sum of concrete checks rather than one person's gut feeling translated into a number.

This doesn't eliminate all subjectivity — "states the main ask within the first two sentences" still requires a judgment call at the margins — but it shrinks the room for disagreement from "we have completely different mental models of professionalism" to "we mostly agree, and disagree only on this one borderline case," which is a much smaller and more manageable gap.
A single scalar score on an undefined quality asks every grader to invent their own definition — decomposing it into concrete sub-criteria is what makes two graders agree.

contentSections.title: Building a rubric criterion by criterion

contentSections.body: A code-review agent's output needs a rubric. The current one-liner: "Gives a good review (0-10)." It's about to get decomposed the same way.

contentSections.intro: Assemble a consistent rubric for grading the code-review agent's output, one criterion at a time.

fields.prompt: What should a coverage criterion check?

options.label: Whether the review 'feels thorough'
Whether the review addresses every function changed in the diff, checked against the actual list of changed functions

feedback.concrete: Right — this gives a grader something to count against a known list, rather than an impression to weigh.
feedback.vague: "Feels thorough" reintroduces exactly the subjectivity the rubric is meant to remove.

fields.prompt: What should a false-positive criterion check?

options.label: The number of issues flagged that a human reviewer confirms are not actually real problems
Whether the review 'seems accurate'

feedback.concrete: Right — a countable number of confirmed-wrong flags is checkable and comparable across reviews.
feedback.vague: 'Seems accurate' is a restated goal, not a check — it's the same problem the rubric exists to fix.

fields.prompt: What should a severity-labeling criterion check?

options.label: Whether each flagged issue is labeled with a severity (blocking / suggestion / nitpick) that a human reviewer agrees with
Whether the review is written in a friendly tone

feedback.concrete: Right — this checks something the review is actually supposed to do (help a human prioritize), against a human's own judgment of severity.
feedback.off-topic: Tone might matter for a different rubric, but it's not what makes a code review useful — mixing it in muddies what this criterion is actually protecting.

contentSections.synthesis: A consistent code-review rubric: coverage (every changed function addressed, checked against the diff), false-positive rate (flagged issues a human confirms aren't real problems), and severity accuracy (each flag's severity label matches a human reviewer's judgment) — three concrete, checkable sub-scores instead of one impression-based 0-10.

contentSections.body: Notice each of the three criteria above still requires a human judgment call somewhere — confirming whether a flagged issue is real, agreeing or disagreeing with a severity label — but the judgment call is now narrow and specific ("is this one flagged issue actually a real problem?") rather than global and vague ("was this a good review?"). That narrowing is the entire value of a rubric: it doesn't remove human judgment, it shrinks each individual judgment down to something two people are far more likely to agree on.
A good rubric doesn't eliminate judgment calls — it shrinks each one down to something narrow and concrete enough that two graders are likely to agree.

title: Model-as-judge, and its systematic biases
description: Using a model to grade another model's output at scale, and the specific, predictable ways that grading tends to go wrong.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what model-as-judge grading is for and why it's used
Identify systematic biases model-as-judge grading is prone to

contentSections.title: Grading three hundred summaries by hand is not happening every week

contentSections.body: A team has a solid, decomposed rubric for grading their document-summarization agent — the kind from the previous lesson. Applying it by hand to their 300-case eval set takes a person most of a day. They want to run this eval every time they change the prompt, which they do several times a week. Hand-grading doesn't scale to that cadence.

contentSections.question: The rubric itself is already solid and decomposed — that part isn't the bottleneck. What's the actual constraint stopping this team from re-checking their eval set every time they tweak the prompt?
contentSections.answer: Raw human grading time. A person applying even a good rubric by hand to 300 cases takes most of a day — that cost, repeated every time the prompt changes, is what makes frequent iteration impractical, not any flaw in the rubric itself.
contentSections.hint: The rubric quality isn't in question here — think about what scales and what doesn't when a human has to apply it by hand, over and over.

contentSections.body:
**Model-as-judge** means using another model call — often, but not always, a more capable model than the one being graded — to apply the rubric to each output and produce a score, instead of a human doing it by hand. This is the thing that makes rubric grading practical at the volume and frequency real iteration needs: a rubric a human wrote once can be applied by a model hundreds of times in minutes, at a fraction of the cost of hand-grading, every time a change needs checking.

It isn't magic, and it isn't a replacement for having a good rubric in the first place — a model-as-judge applying a vague rubric ("is this professional? 0-5") reproduces the exact same inconsistency a vague rubric produces with human graders, just faster and less visibly. What it's genuinely good for is applying an already-decomposed, concrete rubric at scale, freeing human grading time for the smaller, harder job of checking whether the judge itself is trustworthy — which is the next lesson's entire subject.
Model-as-judge exists to apply an already-good rubric at a scale and frequency hand-grading can't sustain — it doesn't fix a bad rubric, it just applies it faster.

contentSections.title: The judge likes long answers and its own writing style

contentSections.body: A team compares two versions of their summarization agent using a model judge. Version A produces tight, 3-sentence summaries. Version B produces longer, 8-sentence summaries that repeat some information for emphasis. The judge consistently scores B higher, even on cases where a human reviewer prefers A's conciseness.

contentSections.code:
Judge prompt (excerpt):

"Rate this summary's quality from 1-10, considering thoroughness, clarity, and completeness."
contentSections.question: What's the likely, well-documented flaw in relying on this judge's scores to compare A and B?

options.label: Model-as-judge scoring has a documented tendency toward length bias — longer, more elaborated answers often score higher independent of whether the extra length adds real value, and a rubric that rewards 'thoroughness' and 'completeness' without a length or concision check can amplify this
There's no flaw — a judge favoring the longer answer is a neutral, unbiased assessment of thoroughness
The flaw is that a model should never be used to judge another model's output under any circumstances

feedback.length-bias: Right. Length bias is one of the most consistently documented model-as-judge tendencies — longer answers often get rewarded for the appearance of thoroughness even when a human reviewer, given the same two answers, prefers the shorter one.
feedback.no-flaw: This treats a well-documented systematic bias as if it were a neutral, correct read of quality — which is exactly the trap. The judge favoring length isn't the same as length actually being better here, as the human reviewer's disagreement shows.
feedback.never-judge: Too strong — model-as-judge is genuinely useful (the previous lesson's whole point), the issue is a specific, known bias in this particular judge setup that needs to be checked for and corrected, not a reason to abandon the approach entirely.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A rubric criterion like 'thoroughness' and 'completeness' with no explicit concision or length constraint gives a judge every reason to reward more text, since more text can always claim to cover more ground — regardless of whether the additional length actually serves the reader. The fix isn't to stop using a judge; it's to know this bias exists and either add an explicit concision criterion or specifically check the judge's agreement with humans on length-varying pairs (the next lesson's topic).

contentSections.body:
A short, non-exhaustive list of documented model-as-judge biases worth knowing by name, because each one calls for a different countermeasure:

- **Length bias** — favoring longer answers, addressed by an explicit concision criterion or length-normalized comparison.
- **Position bias** — when shown two answers to compare, favoring whichever one appears first (or last) in the prompt, addressed by running the comparison both ways and checking for consistency.
- **Self-preference bias** — a judge from the same model family as the one being graded can favor that family's stylistic habits over a genuinely better answer from a different model, addressed by being cautious about using a model to judge its own outputs, or its own family's, without a check against human judgment.
- **Superficial-polish bias** — rewarding confident tone, formatting, and fluency over substantive correctness, addressed by rubric criteria that check specific facts and claims, not overall impression.

None of these mean model-as-judge is unusable — they mean it needs the same skepticism any measurement tool needs before being trusted, which is exactly what the next lesson builds.
Model-as-judge grading has specific, well-documented biases — length, position, self-preference, superficial polish — each with a known countermeasure, not a reason to avoid the approach entirely.

title: Checking your grader against humans
description: Measuring how well an automated grader agrees with human judgment, and what to do when it doesn't.

learningObjectives.text: Design a check of an automated grader's agreement with human judgment
Decide what to do when a grader's disagreement with humans reveals a pattern

contentSections.title: The grader that nobody ever double-checked

contentSections.body: A team has used a model-as-judge grader for their support-response agent for four months. It's never once been compared against what a human would actually say about the same outputs. They assume it's fine because nobody's complained. When they finally hand-score 50 of the same responses the judge already scored, the judge and the humans disagree on 14 of them — nearly a third.

contentSections.scenario: The team is unsettled: four months of tracked progress were measured by a grader whose accuracy was never checked against anything.
contentSections.question: What does a grader whose agreement with humans has never been measured actually give you?

options.label: A trustworthy signal, since the grader is applying a rubric consistently every time

A consistent number, but not necessarily a meaningful one — consistency (the grader scores the same input the same way) is a different property from accuracy (the grader's scores agree with what a human would actually conclude)
Nothing useful at all — an unchecked grader should be discarded entirely

feedback.consistent-not-accurate: Right. A model-as-judge grader can be perfectly consistent — the same input reliably gets the same score — while still being wrong relative to what a human would actually judge. Consistency and accuracy are separate properties, and only measuring against real human judgment checks the second one.
feedback.trustworthy: This conflates the two properties directly — consistency doesn't imply accuracy, and this team's eventual 14-out-of-50 disagreement rate shows exactly why that assumption doesn't hold.
feedback.useless: Too strong in the other direction — an unchecked grader isn't necessarily useless, it's just unverified. Some unchecked graders turn out fine; the point is you don't know which kind you have until you check.

contentSections.mechanism: A grader can be a perfectly reliable measuring instrument that measures the wrong thing — consistently applying a flawed rubric, or consistently exhibiting one of the previous lesson's biases — and nothing about its own internal consistency reveals that. Only a direct comparison against independent human judgment can.

contentSections.body:
The check itself is simple to describe, if not always simple to schedule: take a sample of outputs the grader has already scored, have one or more humans independently score the same outputs using the same rubric, and measure how often they agree. A meaningful sample is usually in the range of several dozen to a hundred — the same sample-size logic from earlier in this phase applies here too; checking against five cases won't reliably reveal a systematic bias.

What counts as "good enough" agreement isn't one universal number — it depends on how much the grader's number will be relied on, same as the sample-size decisions from the first module of this phase. But regardless of the threshold, the check itself — measuring real agreement rather than assuming it — is what turns a grader from a plausible-sounding assumption into something with actual evidence behind it.
A grader's internal consistency says nothing about its accuracy — only a direct, sufficiently sized comparison against independent human judgment does.

contentSections.title: Fourteen disagreements aren't random

contentSections.body: The same team looks closer at their 14 disagreements. Twelve of the fourteen are cases where the judge scored a longer response higher and the human scored a shorter, more direct one higher. The other two look like unrelated one-off disagreements.

contentSections.scenario: 14 disagreements out of 50: 12 follow a length pattern (judge favors longer), 2 don't follow any visible pattern.
contentSections.question: Given this breakdown, which responses are reasonable next steps?

items.label: Add an explicit concision or length-appropriateness criterion to the rubric, since the pattern points directly at the length bias named in the previous lesson
Re-run the judge on the same 50 cases to see if the pattern is stable, not a one-time fluke
Treat the 2 unrelated disagreements as automatically not worth investigating, since they're a small minority
Discard the model-as-judge approach entirely and go back to full hand-grading permanently

explanation.add-concision: Applicable — a pattern this clear (12 of 14 following one known bias) points directly at a specific, fixable gap in the rubric, not at the grading approach being fundamentally broken.
explanation.rerun-judge: Applicable — confirming the pattern is stable, not a one-off sampling artifact in this particular batch of 50, is a reasonable and cheap next step before making changes.
explanation.ignore-two: Not automatically reasonable — a small number of unexplained disagreements is worth at least a quick look, even if it turns out to be genuine noise; dismissing them without looking is its own kind of unchecked assumption.
explanation.discard-grader: An overreaction — the pattern found is fixable (add a concision criterion, re-check), which is a much smaller and more useful response than abandoning an approach that mostly works and scales far better than full hand-grading.

contentSections.synthesis: A clear pattern in the disagreements is more useful than the raw disagreement rate alone — 14/50 sounds like a flat accuracy number, but 12 of those 14 pointing at one known, nameable, fixable bias turns this from 'the grader is unreliable' into 'the grader has one specific, addressable gap.'

contentSections.body: This is the actual payoff of checking a grader against humans: not just a pass/fail verdict on whether to trust it, but a diagnosis of *how* it's wrong, when it is. Look at disagreements as a set, not one at a time — a pattern (favors length, favors a specific phrasing style, consistently misses a particular category of error) points to a specific fix, usually a rubric adjustment or an explicit instruction to the judge to counter the known bias. Scattered, unpatterned disagreement is a different and harder signal — it may mean the rubric itself still has genuinely subjective criteria left in it, worth revisiting with the previous lesson's decomposition approach.
Look at grader disagreements with humans as a set — a pattern points to a specific, fixable gap; scattered disagreement points back at the rubric itself.

title: Grading process, not just final answer
description: Extending grading beyond the final output to check the reasoning and steps that produced it, and where that extra depth is worth the cost.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what grading a process, not just a final output, can catch that outcome grading can't
Design a process-grading check for a given multi-step agent task

contentSections.title: The right answer, reached by luck

contentSections.body: A financial-analysis agent is asked whether a company's quarterly numbers support a loan approval. It answers "approve" — the correct call, matching what a human analyst concluded. Its trace shows it reached that answer by misreading the revenue figure (using last quarter's number instead of this quarter's) and then, separately, misjudging the debt ratio in the company's favor — two errors that happened to cancel out and land on the right final call anyway.

contentSections.question: An outcome-only grader checking only the final "approve"/"don't approve" label would score this run a full pass. Is that score actually telling you the agent's reasoning is trustworthy?
contentSections.answer: No. The final label happens to match the correct answer, but it got there through two separate, real errors that happened to cancel out this time. Nothing about outcome-only grading can distinguish this from a run that reasoned soundly — it only ever looks at where the run landed, not how it got there.
contentSections.hint: Ask what an outcome-only grader can and can't see about the two-step reasoning that produced this particular answer.

contentSections.body:
This connects directly back to the outcome/process/cost distinction from earlier in this phase, applied specifically to grading rather than to measurement design in general. An outcome-only grader would score this response a full pass — "approve" matches the correct answer. But the reasoning that produced it is broken in two separate places, and got lucky. The next case with the same two errors won't necessarily have them cancel out the same way.

**Process grading** checks the reasoning steps themselves, not just where they landed: were the figures pulled correctly, was each intermediate judgment sound, did the chain of reasoning actually support the final conclusion, or did the conclusion happen to be right despite a broken chain. This matters most exactly where it's hardest to notice — cases where errors compound or cancel in a way that produces a correct-looking final answer anyway, which outcome grading structurally cannot catch, by definition, since it only ever looks at the end.
A correct final answer reached through broken reasoning is invisible to outcome-only grading — process grading is the only thing that catches errors that happen to cancel out.

contentSections.title: Grading every step is not always worth it

contentSections.body: A team hears about process grading and decides to grade every single intermediate step of every agent run against a rubric — for a simple three-step lookup-and-format agent that rarely fails and costs almost nothing to get wrong when it does.

contentSections.scenario: Think about the actual cost-benefit here before reading on: a three-step, low-stakes, rarely-wrong agent, versus the earlier financial-analysis agent whose errors can cancel out and whose mistakes are expensive.
contentSections.question: Roughly what fraction of agent tasks in a typical portfolio genuinely justify the added cost of full process grading, versus being fine with outcome grading alone?
contentSections.explanation: There's no precise universal number — this is meant to build the right instinct, not memorize a statistic. But a reasonable informal estimate is a minority, often well under half: process grading is worth its extra cost specifically for tasks that are high-stakes, multi-step in a way errors could compound or cancel, or where you've already seen outcome grading pass something that was actually reasoned badly. A simple, low-stakes, rarely-wrong task usually doesn't need it.

contentSections.body:
Process grading costs more: it needs a trace with real reasoning captured (not just input/output), a rubric for each meaningful step rather than one for the final answer, and either more human grading time or more model-judge calls per run. That cost is worth paying specifically when:

- **The stakes of a wrong answer are high** — a loan decision, a medical-adjacent recommendation, anything where being wrong is expensive or hard to reverse.
- **The task is multi-step enough that errors can compound or cancel** — a single-lookup task has little room for this; a multi-step analysis has a lot.
- **Outcome grading has already been caught passing something that shouldn't have** — direct evidence, from your own eval set, that the final answer alone isn't a reliable enough signal.

For a simple, low-stakes, rarely-wrong task, outcome grading alone is usually the right amount of rigor — adding process grading everywhere, regardless of stakes, spends grading budget on tasks that don't need it while potentially under-investing in the few that genuinely do.
Process grading is worth its extra cost for high-stakes, multi-step tasks where errors can compound or cancel — not a default to apply everywhere regardless of what's actually at stake.

title: Design graders for eight output types
description: Eight drills applying this module's full toolkit — exact-match's limits, rubric decomposition, judge biases, human-agreement checks, and process grading — to new grading scenarios.

learningObjectives.text: Apply grading-approach selection, rubric design, and grader-checking judgment to new agent output types

contentSections.title: Eight drills

contentSections.body: No new concepts here — the same toolkit from the five lessons, run against grading scenarios you haven't seen yet.

The habit worth keeping: match the grading approach to the task's actual shape, decompose vague criteria into concrete ones, know your judge's biases, check it against real humans, and grade the reasoning when the stakes and the task's shape justify it.

title: Build a grader and validate it against your own judgement
description: Write a decomposed rubric, apply it with a model-as-judge, and measure how well it agrees with your own hand-scoring on fifty real examples.

learningObjectives.text: Build a rubric-based grader and measure its agreement against human-scored examples

contentSections.title: The lab

contentSections.body: Every idea in this module — knowing when exact match is enough, decomposing vague criteria into concrete ones, using a judge at scale while knowing its biases, and checking a grader against real human judgment — was building toward one concrete artifact: a grader whose agreement with your own judgment you've actually measured, not just assumed.

contentSections.title: A grader validated against fifty hand-scored examples
contentSections.brief: Pick a real agent task with free-text or otherwise non-exact-match output — ideally the same agent and eval set from the previous two modules' labs. Write a decomposed rubric, apply it (by a model-as-judge, or by hand if you don't have model access set up, simulating the judge role yourself on a delay) to at least fifty outputs, then independently hand-score the same fifty against the same rubric and measure agreement.
contentSections.deliverable: A written rubric with concrete, decomposed criteria; grader scores and independent human scores for the same fifty examples; a measured agreement rate; and a short analysis of any disagreement pattern found, with the specific fix applied in response.

stages.title: Write the rubric
stages.instructions: Take the task's current vague success description and decompose it into 3-5 concrete, checkable criteria, the way lesson two demonstrates. Confirm each criterion is closer to a yes/no or a count than to an overall impression.
stages.checkpoint: A rubric with concrete criteria, none of which are a single undefined 0-5 or 0-10 scale on an undecomposed quality.

stages.title: Grade fifty outputs two ways
stages.instructions: Apply the rubric to fifty real outputs (from your eval set, or generate fifty by running the agent) using a model-as-judge. Separately and independently — without looking at the judge's scores first — hand-score the same fifty outputs yourself against the identical rubric.
stages.checkpoint: Two complete, independent score sets for the same fifty outputs, with the human scoring genuinely done before looking at the judge's results.

stages.title: Measure agreement and diagnose disagreement
stages.instructions: Compare the two score sets. Calculate a simple agreement rate (how many of the fifty the judge and you scored the same or close enough to count as agreement, by your own stated definition of 'close enough'). For any disagreements, look for a pattern — does it resemble one of the named biases from lesson three (length, position, self-preference, polish)?
stages.checkpoint: A calculated agreement rate and a written note on whether disagreements show a pattern or look scattered.

stages.title: Apply a fix and re-check a fresh sample
stages.instructions: If a pattern emerged, make one concrete change to the rubric or judge instructions to address it. Re-check against at least a handful of fresh examples not part of the original fifty to see whether the fix helped.
stages.checkpoint: A stated fix (or a stated conclusion that no fix was needed, with reasoning) and a fresh mini-check of its effect.

rubric.criterion: The rubric is decomposed, not a single vague scale
rubric.meets: Each criterion is concrete and checkable — closer to a yes/no or a count than to an undefined quality on a numeric scale.

rubric.criterion: Fifty outputs were graded independently by both the judge and a human
rubric.meets: The human scoring was genuinely done before, or without reference to, the judge's scores — not adjusted after seeing them.

rubric.criterion: An actual agreement rate is calculated and stated
rubric.meets: A specific number (or fraction) is reported, with a stated definition of what counts as agreement.

rubric.criterion: Disagreements are analyzed as a set, not dismissed individually
rubric.meets: The analysis looks for a pattern across all disagreements, checking against the named biases from lesson three where relevant.

rubric.criterion: A concrete fix (or a reasoned decision not to fix) is documented
rubric.meets: If a pattern was found, a specific rubric or instruction change is described; if not, the reasoning for treating the disagreement as unpatterned is stated.

rubric.criterion: The fix was re-checked, not just assumed to work
rubric.meets: A fresh mini-check, even a small one, tests whether the applied fix actually changed the judge's behavior in the intended direction.

contentSections.body: A grader only earns trust once its agreement with real human judgment has actually been measured, not assumed — this lab exists to produce that measurement, and to close at least one real gap it finds.

The agent's answer is subtly incorrect and the grader caught it
The reference answer needs to be deleted

0-5 scales are always too narrow a range to be useful
It's actually graded consistently; the inconsistency is imagined

options.label: Length bias — a well-documented tendency to favor more elaborated answers independent of whether the length adds real value
Evidence the judge is unusually accurate and thorough
Proof model-as-judge grading should never be used

options.label: Consistency and accuracy are separate properties — a grader can consistently apply a flawed rubric or a systematic bias and never reveal that through its own consistency
Consistency is actually sufficient, and no further check is needed
Consistency only matters for exact-match grading, not for judges

Imagined cases are always too easy for the agent
There's no real blind spot as long as there are enough imagined cases

There's no gap — hard cases are the most rigorous kind to include

Whatever the cheapest storage tier allows by default
A fixed 30-day window that applies to every kind of trace equally

questions.explanation: From Seeing What It Did — a retention window grounded in real investigation timelines, weighed against real sensitivity, is a reasoned decision; a round number chosen because it sounds cautious isn't.

title: Running evals as part of your workflow
description: Why an eval set that only gets run 'when someone remembers' fails at the one job it exists to do, and what it means to wire it into the actual development loop.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an eval set run only occasionally fails to catch regressions in practice
Identify the points in a development workflow where an eval run should happen automatically

contentSections.title: Nobody happened to rerun it that week

contentSections.body: A team has a genuinely good, well-sourced thirty-case eval set for their invoice-processing agent — everything the last two modules of this phase argued for. They run it after big changes, when they remember to. A small tool-call refactor, three weeks ago, quietly broke handling for multi-line-item invoices. Nobody reran the eval set after that refactor specifically — the next full run happens three weeks later, by which point dozens of real invoices have gone through wrong.

contentSections.scenario: The eval set itself would have caught this immediately — a multi-line-item case is right there in the boring band. The team isn't confused about whether it would have caught it; they're confused about why it didn't.
contentSections.question: What actually failed here?

options.label: The eval set's coverage — it must not have had a multi-line-item case after all

The workflow — a good eval set that only runs when someone remembers to run it is only as reliable as everyone's memory, and a routine refactor is exactly the kind of change that doesn't feel eval-worthy in the moment
The refactor itself was simply too subtle for any eval set to catch

feedback.workflow: Right. The set had the coverage — the scenario says so directly. What broke is that having a good eval set and actually running it at the right moments are two different things, and this team only had the first.
feedback.coverage: The scenario states the eval set would have caught this — the gap isn't in what the set covers, it's in when it actually gets run.
feedback.too-subtle: Nothing about a multi-line-item invoice regression is inherently hard to catch — it's exactly the kind of thing a boring-band eval case exists to catch. The miss was about timing, not subtlety.

contentSections.mechanism: An eval set only catches a regression at the moment it's actually run — a great eval set run three weeks after the change that broke something has let three weeks of real, uncaught failures happen in between. 'Run it when someone remembers' quietly depends on every change feeling eval-worthy in the moment, and a routine refactor rarely does.

contentSections.body:
This is the same shape of problem the earlier module on operating agents over time named for maintenance in general: a plan that depends on someone remembering, during a busy week, to do the optional-feeling thing, is a plan that works right up until the week it doesn't. For evals specifically, the fix is the same one that made automated testing useful for regular software: **run the eval set automatically, at defined points, not manually when it occurs to someone.**

The natural points to wire it into:

- **Before merging any change** that touches the prompt, the tools, the model version, or the agent's logic — the same discipline as running a test suite before merge.
- **On a schedule**, even with no code changes, to catch drift from outside the codebase (an upstream API changing shape, a model provider updating a 'latest' alias) — covered further in lesson three.
- **Before any deploy**, as a final check independent of whatever ran at merge time, in case something changed between merge and deploy.

None of this requires sophisticated infrastructure to start — even a single command a person runs and reads the output of, done at every one of these points without skipping, beats a great eval set that only runs when someone happens to think of it.
An eval set only catches a regression at the moment it's run — 'when someone remembers' means real failures get however many days or weeks pass before someone happens to remember.

contentSections.title: Which changes actually need a rerun

contentSections.body: A teammate pushes back on running the full eval set before every merge: "Half our merges are typo fixes in comments or README updates — running a 30-case eval set for those is wasted time and money."

contentSections.question: Is the teammate's objection actually a reason to abandon 'eval before every merge,' or does it point at a more precise version of the same rule?
contentSections.answer: A more precise version. The rule was never really "every single merge, no matter what it touches" — it's "every merge that could plausibly change agent behavior." A comment or README change can't change what the agent does at runtime, so skipping the eval there isn't cutting a corner, it's correctly scoping the rule to changes that touch the prompt, the tools, the model configuration, or the agent's logic.
contentSections.hint: Ask what actually determines whether a change could affect the agent's behavior — the file it touches, or just 'any merge at all.'

contentSections.body:
The useful distinction isn't "always run evals" versus "run them when convenient" — it's being precise about *which* changes can plausibly affect behavior. A change to the system prompt, the tool definitions, the model version or provider, the agent's control logic (how it decides what to do next), or its retrieval/context sources are all behavior-relevant and deserve an eval run before merging. A documentation fix, a logging-only change, or a refactor that's provably behavior-preserving (same logic, cleaner code) generally isn't.

The risk in drawing that line is being too generous about what counts as "provably behavior-preserving" — the multi-line-item regression from the first pod started as exactly that kind of refactor, one that looked purely internal until it wasn't. When genuinely unsure whether a change could affect behavior, the cheap default is to run the eval anyway; the cost of an unnecessary run is small compared to the cost of a missed regression.
The rule isn't 'eval every merge' — it's 'eval every merge that could plausibly affect behavior,' and when genuinely unsure, the cheap default is to run it anyway.

title: The prompt change that fixed one thing and broke three
description: Why verifying a fix by rerunning only the case it targeted misses the side effects it can have on everything else, and why the full eval set is the actual unit of verification.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why rerunning only the originally-failing case after a fix can miss new regressions the fix introduced elsewhere
Apply full-eval-set verification as the standard check for any prompt or logic change

contentSections.title: Case #14 passes. Cases #3, #9, and #22 quietly stop

contentSections.body: A team's research agent fails eval case #14: it cites a source it never actually read. They add a firm instruction to the system prompt: "Only cite a source if you have directly quoted or paraphrased its content in your response." They rerun case #14. It passes. They merge. The next full eval run, days later, shows cases #3, #9, and #22 — previously passing, unrelated to citation behavior — now fail.

contentSections.code:
Verification note attached to the merge:

"Fixed case #14 (citing unread sources).
Added prompt instruction requiring quote/paraphrase before citation.
Reran case #14: PASS.
Merging."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this verification, independent of whether the instruction itself was a reasonable idea?

options.label: Only the originally-failing case was rerun — nothing checked whether the new, firmer instruction changed behavior on the other twenty-nine cases in the set, which is exactly where the new failures showed up
There's no flaw; a passing rerun of the exact case that was failing is sufficient verification for any change
The flaw is that the new instruction should never have been added to the prompt at all

feedback.narrow-rerun: Right. A firm new instruction added to a shared system prompt doesn't stay contained to the one case it was written for — it changes the agent's behavior on every case that prompt applies to, and only running the full set would have shown the new instruction being too strict elsewhere.
feedback.no-flaw: This is the exact trap the exercise is naming — a passing rerun of one case says nothing about whether a shared, global change (a system prompt instruction) affected any of the other cases sharing that same prompt.
feedback.shouldnt-add: The instruction wasn't necessarily a bad idea — it correctly fixed case #14. The flaw is entirely in how it was verified, not in whether it should exist.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A system prompt is shared context for every case, not a per-case setting — an instruction added to fix one case's specific failure applies to all twenty-nine other cases too, whether or not it was written with them in mind. "Only cite if directly quoted or paraphrased" turned out to be too strict for three cases where a source was legitimately cited as general background support rather than direct quotation. Rerunning only case #14 could never have revealed that, because case #14 was never where the new failures were going to show up.

contentSections.body:
This connects directly to the earlier lesson on module-two's eval-set honesty: fixing a case by patching its exact literal wording, rather than the general issue, is one way a fix goes wrong. This is the companion failure, on the *verification* side rather than the fix side: even a reasonably general fix can have side effects on cases that had nothing to do with the original failure, because most fixes to a prompt, a tool definition, or shared agent logic aren't scoped to one case — they're global changes applied to a global input.

The practical rule: **the unit of verification for any change is the full eval set, not the case that motivated the change.** Rerunning just the originally-failing case answers "did I fix this one thing," which is a real and useful question, but a different and smaller one than "did I break anything else while fixing it" — and only the full set answers the second.
A fix to shared prompt or logic isn't scoped to the case that motivated it — only rerunning the full eval set reveals whether it broke something the original failing case never touched.

contentSections.title: Why a shared prompt has this blast radius

contentSections.body: A teammate asks the obvious follow-up: why would tightening a citation rule for one specific failure mode (citing unread sources) affect cases about something else entirely, like source recency or summary length?

contentSections.scenario: The new instruction: "Only cite a source if you have directly quoted or paraphrased its content in your response." Three previously-passing cases now fail: one where a source was cited as general background context without a direct quote (now under-cited and flagged as unsupported); one where the added instruction's extra prompt length pushed a different section of the instructions out of the model's effective attention; one that was unrelated and turns out to be ordinary run-to-run variance, not the instruction's fault.
contentSections.question: Which of these are legitimate, real mechanisms by which one prompt change can affect seemingly unrelated cases?

items.label: The new rule, read literally, disqualifies a legitimate citation style (background support) the eval set didn't originally test for narrowly enough to distinguish from the bug being fixed
A longer, denser system prompt can shift how much weight the model effectively gives to other instructions elsewhere in the same prompt
Every regression that shows up right after a prompt change is caused by that change
Confirming which of the three failures are real (caused by the change) versus variance requires the same repeated-runs comparison from earlier in this phase, not just one before/after run

explanation.scope-too-strict: Applicable — a rule written to fix one narrow failure mode can be broader than intended, catching legitimate cases that only superficially resemble the bug.
explanation.attention-competition: Applicable — this is a real, documented dynamic: instructions compete for a model's effective attention within a prompt, so adding one can measurably change how strongly others are followed, even with no logical contradiction between them.
explanation.always-real-cause: Not applicable — this module's earlier lessons in this phase established that a single before/after comparison can't distinguish a real effect from ordinary variance; assuming every co-occurring failure is caused by the change skips that check.
explanation.verify-with-multiple-runs: Applicable — exactly the variance-aware verification habit from the first module of this phase, now applied specifically to comparing eval runs before and after a change.

contentSections.synthesis: A prompt change can cause real regressions through more than one mechanism (an overly broad rule, attention competing with other instructions) — and separately, not every co-occurring failure is actually caused by the change at all. Both of those are reasons the full eval set, run enough times to separate signal from variance, is the only trustworthy check.

contentSections.body: None of this is a reason to avoid touching shared prompts or logic — it's a reason to treat every such change the way this phase has been building toward treating everything else: define what should happen, make the change, then verify against the full, real measure (the whole eval set, run enough times to be confident) rather than against the narrow thing that prompted the change in the first place.

A prompt change can regress unrelated cases through more than one real mechanism — an overly broad rule, or competition for the model's attention — which is exactly why the full eval set, not just the motivating case, is the real check.

title: Model version changes under you
description: Why an agent's behavior can shift with no code change on your side, and how eval discipline needs to account for a dependency that updates itself.

learningObjectives.text: Explain how a model version change can cause an eval regression with no change in the team's own codebase
Evaluate the tradeoffs between pinning a model version and tracking the latest version automatically

contentSections.title: Nothing in the git log, everything in the behavior

contentSections.body: A team's eval pass rate drops from 91% to 79% between two scheduled Tuesday runs. Nothing merged in between — the git log is empty for that window. Their model configuration references "claude-latest" rather than a specific dated version, and the provider shipped a new default version three days before the second run.

contentSections.scenario: The team's first instinct is to look for a code change they missed, because that's usually where regressions come from.
contentSections.question: Given an empty git log, what's actually the most likely cause?

options.label: A code change so subtle it left no trace in version control
The model configuration points at a moving target ("latest") rather than a fixed version, so the model itself changed underneath the agent with zero commits on the team's side
The eval set itself must have changed between the two runs

feedback.moving-target: Right. A configuration that always resolves to whatever the provider currently calls 'latest' means the actual model answering requests can change without a single line of the team's own code changing — which is exactly what an empty git log alongside a real behavior shift points to.
feedback.invisible-code: Version control doesn't miss committed changes — if the git log is genuinely empty for that window, the explanation isn't a hidden code change, it's something that changed outside the codebase entirely.
feedback.eval-changed: Nothing in the scenario suggests the eval set itself was touched — and even if it's worth double-checking, the far more common cause of a git-log-empty regression, especially with a 'latest' alias in play, is exactly this kind of external model change.

contentSections.mechanism: Referencing a model by a moving alias like 'latest' means the actual model version is a dependency the team doesn't control the timing of — the same category of risk the earlier module on operating agents over time named for any external dependency: it can drift or change with zero signal in your own commit history.

contentSections.body:
This is a direct continuation of a topic covered from the maintenance angle earlier in this track — here it's specifically an evaluation problem: **a regression with an empty change log, on the team's own side, is the signature of an external dependency changing, and a model version is one of the most common ones.** The practical response has two parts:

1. **Notice it fast.** This is exactly what a scheduled eval run (lesson one) catches that a merge-triggered run alone wouldn't — no merge happened, so only a run on a schedule, independent of any code change, would have caught this at all.
2. **Diagnose it correctly.** Before assuming a code bug, check whether the model configuration references a moving target, and check the provider's own changelog for a version update around the time of the drop. Chasing a code-side bug that doesn't exist wastes real time when the actual cause is external.
A regression with an empty change log on your own side, right after a real eval-score drop, is the signature of an external dependency — often a model version — changing underneath you.

contentSections.title: Pin it and miss improvements, or float it and risk drift

contentSections.body: Having found the cause, the team debates the fix. One person wants to pin to an exact, dated model version and never move automatically. Another argues that means missing real improvements and eventually running an officially deprecated model with no support.

contentSections.scenario: Two options on the table: pin to an exact dated version and update only deliberately; or track "latest" and accept whatever the provider currently serves.
contentSections.question: Which of these are real, legitimate costs of each approach — not exaggerations, but genuine trade-offs worth weighing?

items.label: Pinning risks eventually running a version the provider stops serving entirely, forcing an unplanned, rushed migration
Pinning means missing quality or cost improvements a newer version might offer, until someone deliberately evaluates and migrates
Tracking "latest" means the agent's behavior can shift on a schedule the team doesn't control, with no chance to evaluate the new version before it's live
Pinning is always strictly worse than tracking latest, since it's more manual work

explanation.pin-deprecation: Applicable — a pinned version doesn't stay supported forever; without a deliberate migration plan, a deprecation deadline can force a rushed move under time pressure, which the earlier module on operating agents over time covered directly.
explanation.pin-missed-gains: Applicable — a genuinely better or cheaper newer version sits unused until someone actively decides to evaluate and adopt it, which is a real, if smaller, cost.
explanation.latest-drift: Applicable — this is exactly what happened in this lesson's opening scenario: the model changed with zero warning and zero chance to evaluate first.
explanation.pin-always-worse: Not applicable — this frames it as one-sided, but the trade-off is genuine in both directions; "more manual work" is the cost of pinning, and "uncontrolled, unevaluated changes" is the cost of not pinning, and which matters more depends on the task's stakes.

contentSections.synthesis: There's no option that avoids trade-offs entirely. A reasonable middle path many teams land on: pin to a specific version for anything running in production, and deliberately evaluate new versions on the full eval set — using the comparison discipline from earlier lessons in this phase — before choosing to migrate, rather than either freezing forever or floating automatically.

contentSections.body: Whichever approach a team picks, the eval set is what makes it a safe choice rather than a guess either way: pinning without ever re-evaluating newer versions means potentially running something worse than what's available; floating without ever pausing to evaluate a new version before it goes live means finding out about a regression from users instead of from a scheduled eval run. The version-pinning decision and the eval-running discipline from this module aren't separate — the second is what makes either version of the first one safe.
Pinning and floating both carry real, different costs — the eval set, run and compared deliberately before any version change goes live, is what makes either choice a safe one rather than a guess.

title: Comparing runs meaningfully despite variance
description: Comparing two eval runs the same way this phase already learned to comparing individual cases — with repetition, and by looking at which cases actually flipped.

learningObjectives.text: Design a comparison between two eval-set runs that accounts for ordinary variance
Interpret a case-level comparison between two runs, not just the aggregate score delta

contentSections.title: 82% versus 85%, and also 80% versus 84% on the identical code

contentSections.body: A team runs their eval set once against the current version (82%) and once against a candidate new version (85%) and calls the new version an improvement. Out of caution, someone reruns the *exact same* current version again, unchanged: 80%. Then reruns the *exact same* candidate version again: 84%. The two "before" numbers differ by 2 points, and the two "after" numbers differ by 1 point — purely from re-running identical code.

contentSections.scenario: Given that identical code produced an 80%-to-82% spread on its own, just from ordinary variance across reruns, think about what that means for trusting the original 82%-vs-85% comparison.
contentSections.question: Roughly how much of the original 3-point gap (82% to 85%) could plausibly be explained by the same kind of variance already observed (a 2-point spread from reruns of identical code), rather than the new version being genuinely better?
contentSections.explanation: A meaningful share — potentially most or all of it. If identical, unchanged code alone produces a 2-point spread between reruns, a 3-point gap between two *different* versions is not obviously distinguishable from that same variance. This doesn't prove the new version isn't better — it means one run of each version can't establish that on its own.

contentSections.body:
This is the same variance idea from the first module of this phase, now applied specifically to comparing two full eval runs rather than one case. A single run of version A and a single run of version B, compared as one number each, treats both scores as if they were fixed facts — but each one is actually a single draw from a distribution, exactly like a single self-run trial was in the very first lesson of this phase.

The fix is the same shape too: **run each version multiple times** (as many as the stakes justify — a quick internal check might tolerate 2-3 reruns per version, a real ship decision deserves more) and compare the *ranges*, not single point numbers. If version A's rate across several reruns clusters around 80-83% and version B's clusters around 84-86%, with the ranges not overlapping much, that's a real signal. If both ranges span 80-86% and overlap heavily, the single 82-vs-85 comparison that started this was noise dressed up as a result.

A single run of each version, compared as two point numbers, can't be told apart from the ordinary variance a single version shows across its own reruns — compare ranges from repeated runs, not one-off scores.

contentSections.title: Which cases actually flipped, not just the net number

contentSections.body: After running both versions several times each, the team confirms version B is genuinely, reliably better in aggregate — 84% versus 81%, consistently, across reruns. Before shipping, someone asks a different question: which specific cases account for that difference, and did anything get worse along the way?

contentSections.scenario: A case-level diff between version A and version B, aggregated across the repeated runs: 5 cases that reliably failed on A now reliably pass on B; 1 case that reliably passed on A now reliably fails on B; the rest are unchanged or still noisy either way.
contentSections.question: Given this breakdown, which conclusions are actually justified?

items.label: Version B is a net improvement — 5 genuine fixes against 1 genuine new failure is a real, positive trade in aggregate
The 1 newly-failing case is still worth looking at specifically — a reliable, real regression on any single case is worth understanding even inside an overall net-positive change
Once the aggregate number is confirmed as a real, reliable improvement, there's no more value in looking at which specific cases moved
A net-positive aggregate justifies shipping regardless of what the 1 regressed case represents, even without looking at it

explanation.net-positive: Applicable — 5 confirmed fixes against 1 confirmed new failure, verified across repeated runs rather than single point numbers, is a real, legitimate net improvement.
explanation.check-the-one: Applicable — a net-positive change can still be hiding something worth knowing about, especially if the newly-failing case represents a high-stakes or high-frequency real situation rather than a rare edge case.
explanation.aggregate-enough: Not applicable — the aggregate confirms the overall direction, but it can't tell you *what kind* of case regressed, which matters for deciding whether to ship as-is, patch first, or accept the trade knowingly.
explanation.ship-regardless: Not applicable — shipping without even looking at what the one regression represents skips exactly the check that would reveal whether it's a rare edge case (fine to accept) or a common, costly one (worth fixing first).

contentSections.synthesis: A confirmed, real net improvement is still worth decomposing at the case level before shipping — not because the aggregate might be wrong, but because 'net positive' can be true while still containing a specific regression worth knowing about and deciding on deliberately, rather than shipping past unnoticed.

contentSections.body: This is the practical form of the outcome/process distinction from the first module of this phase, applied to comparing versions: the aggregate pass-rate delta is the outcome-level signal, and the case-by-case diff is the process-level detail that explains *how* that outcome was reached. A team that only ever looks at the aggregate number is making the same mistake as a team that only checks whether a flight got booked without looking at how — it's very possible to miss a real, specific new problem sitting inside a genuinely good overall number.
A confirmed net-positive aggregate can still hide a specific regression worth knowing about — the case-level diff is what a single delta number can't show you.

title: A dashboard you'll actually look at
description: Why an elaborate eval dashboard tends to get abandoned within weeks, and what a lightweight report that actually gets read looks like instead.

learningObjectives.text: Identify why an overly elaborate eval dashboard tends to stop being used
Design a minimal eval comparison report that surfaces what a change actually needs to know

contentSections.title: Forty metrics, zero people looking at week three

contentSections.body: A team, energized after wiring evals into their workflow, builds an ambitious dashboard: forty tracked metrics across every case, every band, every model version, with charts for each. Week one, everyone checks it daily. Week three, nobody has opened it in five days — a real regression sits visible on the dashboard, unnoticed, for that entire time.

contentSections.scenario: The dashboard has every number anyone could want. That's exactly what's wrong with it.
contentSections.question: What actually caused the dashboard to stop being checked?

options.label: The team simply lost interest in quality as a priority

Forty metrics is more than a busy person can scan in the few seconds they actually have between other tasks — the dashboard optimized for completeness over the one thing that determines whether it gets checked: how fast someone can answer 'did anything get worse' from it
Dashboards are inherently unreliable and should be replaced with something else entirely

feedback.too-much-friction: Right. This is the same shape of failure as the maintenance-plan problem from earlier in the track: something built for maximum thoroughness, with only one mode, collapses the first time anyone's capacity to engage with it is anything less than ideal — which for a dashboard means every single busy day.
feedback.lost-interest: Nothing in the scenario suggests the team stopped caring about quality — the real regression sitting unnoticed is evidence they'd have wanted to know, if the dashboard had made that easy to see.
feedback.dashboards-bad: The problem isn't the format, it's the design — a dashboard scoped to answer one clear question quickly is a completely different, and much more durable, thing than a forty-metric wall of numbers.

contentSections.mechanism: A tool only helps if it actually gets used, and what determines actual use isn't how much information it contains — it's how fast someone can extract the one answer they need from it, on a day they have very little time to look.

contentSections.body:
This is the eval-dashboard version of the sustainable-maintenance-routine idea from earlier in the track: a plan (or a tool) with only an ambitious, thorough mode fails completely the moment full attention isn't available, rather than degrading gracefully.
